plan: [Value = $25. In a 5-bidder third-price sealed-bid auction, symmetric equilibrium is linear: bid = (4/3) × value (derivation: best-response calculus with opponents using linear bids gives coefficient 4/3). No history to update on. To maximize long-run profit against similar opponents, bid the equilibrium amount, rounded to $0.1.]

[This is a 3rd-price sealed-bid auction with 5 bidders. In such auctions, bidding your true private value is a weakly dominant strategy because if you win your payment equals the 3rd-highest other bid (independent of your own bid, as long as you remain the highest). Values redraw each round but here only one round exists. To maximize long-run expected profit (and here the round profit), I will bid my true value of $3, using the available $0.1 increments to avoid strategic deviation or unnecessary risk.]

[I will bid my true private value of $26. With a third-price rule, overbidding can force paying a third-highest bid that exceeds my value; underbidding reduces win probability and foregoes positive surplus. No history to learn from; truthful bidding balances risk and expected profit in this one-shot game.]

[Third-price, 5 bidders, values iid Uniform[0,49]. In symmetric equilibrium one shows b(v)= (4/3)v (derived via the first-order condition for optimal z and order-statistics of 4 opponents). For v=35 this gives 140/3 ≈ 46.6667. Round to the nearest $0.1 to maximize long-run expected profit.]

[This is a third-price sealed-bid with 5 bidders; if I win I pay the second-highest of the other four bids. My private value is high (45/49) and draws are independent with no history to learn from. Bidding my true value is a safe, aggressive strategy: it maximizes my chance to win when the item is valuable to me while the price paid is set by others' bids, not mine. Given no prior rounds and uniform values, I will bid my value to capture positive expected surplus when others are lower.]
